title: Trump Returns to Correspondents' Dinner with Rambling Speech, Jabs, and a 'Trump 2028' Hat
summary: Three months after a gunman forced its postponement, the White House Correspondents' Association dinner resumed Friday night—and President Donald Trump took the mic for over an hour. His speech was a rambling blend of self-praise, potshots at journalists and celebrities, and dark humor about a third term. "As I said three months ago, the show must go on," Trump began, acknowledging the "attempted mass murder" that could have unfolded in April. But he quickly pivoted to insults, targeting everyone from Jane Fonda to "Barack Hussein Obama." The audience's laughter faded as the jabs piled up, with some comments flirting with racism. Trump also mocked late-night hosts, Democratic politicians, and even his own speechwriters. He expressed pride in the Waldorf Astoria ballroom—formerly his hotel—and questioned the journalism awards, many of which honored reporting critical of his administration. "Do I have a say in those awards?" he asked with a grimace. The most provocative moment came when he joked about a third term, barred by the 22nd Amendment. "Just like my presidency, the second time is always better. And the third time will be better yet." He then donned a red "Trump 2028" cap, claiming he was "only kidding." The event was markedly subdued: a smaller venue, no red carpet, and tight security with ID checks and detection dogs. WHCA president Weijia Jiang struck a defiant note: "We will not be intimidated. We refuse to let an act of violence have the final word." Trump's appearance signaled a complex relationship with the press—one he continues to attack, sue, and bar from events.
why_it_matters: When a leader treats constitutional limits as a punchline and openly mocks journalists at a free‑press dinner, it raises questions about democratic norms. How leaders and the media treat each other affects whether citizens get truthful information and whether rules that protect everyone are taken seriously.

background_read: The White House Correspondents’ Association dinner is an annual Washington tradition where journalists and the sitting president roast each other in a light‑hearted way. President Trump boycotted the event during his first term, making his returns especially charged.

The 22nd Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, ratified in 1951, limits any person to two elected terms as president—a rule introduced after Franklin D. Roosevelt served four terms. Any talk of a third term, even as a joke, stirs strong reactions because it touches on the democratic principle of peaceful transfer of power.

Three months earlier, a gunman had attempted to force entry to the planned dinner, leading to a security overhaul. The revised event had no red carpet, a smaller venue and detection dogs, reflecting a climate of heightened threats.

Weijia Jiang, the WHCA president, is a CBS News correspondent who previously became known for tense exchanges with Trump at press briefings. Her defiant words aimed to show that the press corps would not be silenced by violence or bullying.

perspectives.description: Supporters see Trump’s decision to attend—despite the earlier threat—as a show of strength and resilience. They find his humour entertaining and view his attacks on the media as a justified pushback against biased reporting.

Critics argue the speech trivialised a near‑tragic attack, flouted the Constitution with the third‑term joke, and deepened divisions. Mocking journalists at an event meant to celebrate free speech sends a chilling signal to reporters worldwide.

Presidents have used the dinner for decades to poke fun at themselves and the press. Trump’s appearance shows the tension between his open hostility toward the media and his need for its coverage. The tight security also reflects a broader rise in political violence.

The 2028 joke, even if brushed off as comedy, may embolden talk of challenging term limits. If Trump continues to sue news organisations and bar reporters, watchdogs warn the next generation of journalists could face even harsher obstacles.
